newsitem.title: FRANCE: French cabinet backs tighter anti-racism laws.
newsitem.headline: French cabinet backs tighter anti-racism laws.

text.p: The French cabinet, driven by far- right politician Jean-Marie Le Pen's embrace of racial inequality, backed a plan on Wednesday that would tighten anti-racism laws and increase penalties for racist statements.
The cabinet also approved a proposal to crack down on illegal workers who either lack residence papers or whose employers fail to pay required fees and taxes.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe planned to consult extensively with interested groups before parliament began its deliberations on the anti-racism measure, probably in the first three months of 1997, government spokesman Alain Lamassoure told reporters.
The bill, drafted by Justice Minister Jacques Toubon, has stirred criticism that its language is so broad that it may threaten freedom of speech.
It was drafted after Le Pen, leader of the anti-immigrant National Front party, declared in August, "Yes, I believe in racial inequality, certainly, it's obvious".
Politicians and civic leaders from across the political spectrum denounced his remarks and many urged that he be prosecuted under an 1881 law, updated in 1972, against inciting racial hatred.

But Toubon said the law had to be tightened before it could be used against statements like Le Pen's. The law appears not to cover general verbal attacks, for example, against all foreigners or against immigrants, officials explained.
Under the proposed reform, an individual would no longer have to cite a particular religion or national or ethnic group to be prosecuted for a racist statement.
The measure would punish a racist statement by up to a year in prison and a fine of up to 300,000 francs ($60,000).
Sanctions would increase to two years in jail and a 500,000 franc ($100,000) fine if the remark were judged an incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence.
"In these dangerous times, it is important that we put a stop to these racist actions," Toubon told reporters following the cabinet meeting.

Le Pen, who has in the past dismissed the Nazi gas chambers as a mere detail in the history of World War Two, won 15 percent of the vote in 1995 presidential elections. Juppe has branded him "deeply, almost viscerally racist, anti-Semitic and xenophobic".
Labour Minister Jacques Barrot said the cabinet plan to rein in illicit labour would enable police to better track down employers who violate the law as well as workers.
One of its provisions would ban firms from seeking public contracts if they were convicted of using illicit workers during the previous five years.
Lamassoure estimated the value of black market work in the French economy at 80 billion francs ($15.5 billion) and said 22,000 illegal workers had been uncovered last year.
In 70 percent of the cases, the illegal worker lacked the necessary official paperwork while in just six percent of the cases were illegal immigrants involved, he said.
